1) Schools are not allowed to suppress the 1st Amendment rights of students, meaning that so long as their religious attire, worship, and activities do not interfere with the operations of the school, they are permitted to do it. 2) Schools are allowed to make academic study of religion and religious literature. Such courses must be opt-in and should not be designed to proselytize, and will be scrutinized as such.

3) Anti-discrimination laws state that any public and government institutions may not discriminate based on the criteria of gender, race, or religious creed. If a public building allows access and usage to non-religious groups and restricts use of religious groups, they are in violation of the law.

4) Establishment states that, "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof". That means there may be no federal assertion that any religion is the official religion of the United States of America. Similarly, the ratification of the Constitution ensures that signatory states will adhere to the constitutionally granted rights and ensure that the rights of its citizenry will not be violated. That means no state may issue an assertion that officiates a state religion, and on down the chain.

Thus: "For a law to be considered constitutional under the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment, the law must have a legitimate secular purpose, must not have the primary effect of either advancing or inhibiting religion, and also must not result in an excessive entanglement of government and religion"

Bradfield v. Roberts saw the courts rule that funding to institutions is permissible (even when run by a religious group) if the services it provides are secular.

Even further, the government may supply finance to institutes of higher learning even when they are run by religious groups, for facilities and infrastructure (Tilton v Richardson).
